title: Scholarship payments
summary: BecaPay deposits grants to 15,000 university students through an app. The auditor requires a standard login, the company's own keys and a trail of every change.

requirements.1: {{s1}} lets students sign in with email or with their Google account, and the app receives OAuth 2.0 / OIDC tokens that expire and are renewed with a refresh token.
requirements.2: {{s2}} rejects any call to /pagos with an invalid, expired or foreign-issuer token before it reaches the service.
requirements.3: {{s3}} encrypts the database and backups with company keys that rotate every year, and every use of those keys can be logged.
requirements.4: {{s4}} alerts if someone operates the cloud resources from a suspicious IP address.
requirements.5: {{s5}} shows the auditor who changed a firewall rule or deleted a resource, when and from where.
requirements.6: The payments service runs in the private subnet and only receives calls that slot 2 already validated.
requirements.7: The database stores the scholarship holders' accounts and deposits, encrypted with the slot 3 keys.

s1.explanation: A Cognito user pool adds the Google button, handles the OAuth 2.0 and OIDC exchange, and gives the app ID and access tokens that expire (5 minutes to 1 day) plus a refresh token to get new ones.

s2.explanation: With a JWT authorizer on the route, API Gateway checks the signature, issuer (iss), audience and expiration (exp) and denies the request if any check fails. It reaches the private subnet through a private integration: a VPC link to a load balancer or Cloud Map.

s3.explanation: A customer managed KMS key can rotate on its own, every 365 days unless another period is set, and CloudTrail logs every cryptographic operation with it, such as Decrypt or GenerateDataKey.
s3.hint_cue: company keys that rotate every year

s4.explanation: GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS queries; its MaliciousIPCaller finding warns when someone invokes an AWS API from a known malicious IP address.

s5.explanation: Each CloudTrail event stores who made the request (userIdentity), when (eventTime) and from which IP (sourceIPAddress), and CloudTrail shows resource creation, changes and deletion.

aws-iam.s1: IAM controls who is authenticated and authorized to use AWS resources; it does not offer sign-up or sign-in for the app's students.

aws-nlb.s2: The Network Load Balancer works at layer 4: it picks a target with a hash of protocol, IP and port, without opening the HTTP request that carries the token.

aws-secrets-manager.s3: Secrets Manager stores and rotates secrets, such as database credentials and API keys, and encrypts them with KMS keys; it is not the service that creates and rotates those encryption keys.

aws-inspector.s4: Inspector looks for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure in EC2, ECR images and Lambda; it does not alert on API calls that come from a suspicious IP address.

aws-vpc-flow-logs.s5: VPC Flow Logs capture information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces; they do not say which user changed a firewall rule or who deleted a resource.
